articles.headline: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
articles.teaser: Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into actionIn a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate.

articles.headline: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
articles.teaser: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosingDuring the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK.
articles.originalHeadline: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial

Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country.Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address.

articles.teaser: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young peopleThis should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. articles.headline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.teaser: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair.For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books.To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian.Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak.Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers.
articles.originalHeadline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
